chapters.title: Numbers One to Five
chapters.label: ch:numbers-one-to-five
chapters.canDo: I can say the Sanskrit numerals एक to पञ्च with their dual and gendered forms, and follow पञ्च outward into Punjab, pentagon, and the disputed history of punch.

payoff.summary: Trace pañca out of Sanskrit: into Persian panj-āb, the five waters behind Punjab; into Greek pente in pentagon and pentathlon; and into punch, with the five-ingredients account labelled as common rather than settled.

chapters.title: The Core Verbs
chapters.label: ch:sa-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say that someone is, becomes, goes, comes, eats, sees and knows in Sanskrit; I can name each verb by its dhātu rather than by its present form, say which of the three gaṇa patterns builds its stem, and point at the English word that descends from the same root.

payoff.summary: Say जानाति, name its root ज्ञा and the syllable -ना- its class plants inside the word, run back through the chapter's six verbs as root plus class plus ending, separate the one that is a prefixed form of another, and pair गम्, अद्, पश् and भू with come, eat, inspect and be.

chapters.title: The Mind and the Palm Leaf
chapters.label: ch:sa-mind-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say that someone thinks, understands, reads and writes in Sanskrit; I can name the class that plants -अय- inside a verb, build "understands" out of a prefix and a verb I already had, say what लिख् meant before it meant write, and tell a word worn down by speech (तद्भव) from one carried over whole (तत्सम).

payoff.summary: Say लिखति, give the scratching sense its root carried first, run the chapter's four verbs back as root plus class plus ending — the planted -अय- of चिन्तयति, the अव- prefix and the waking बुध् behind understanding, the plain -a- of पठति and लिखति — sort Bengali lekhā and Hindi cintā into तद्भव and तत्सम, and name the two word-histories that needed a label rather than a claim.

chapters.title: Taking, Asking, Helping, Loving
chapters.label: ch:sa-doing-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say that someone takes, asks, helps and loves in Sanskrit; I can say संस्कृतं मम प्रियम्, build a verb by putting करोति behind a noun, and point at the English word — grab, pray, friend — that each of these four roots also produced.

payoff.summary: Say संस्कृतं मम प्रियम्, give स्निह् its older sense of stickiness and label the disputed snow connection, follow प्रिय west into friend, free and Friday by the p-to-f change that also made pañca into five, run the chapter's four verbs back with grab, pray and comes beside them, and sort प्रिय against Hindi piyā as तत्सम against तद्भव — then place पञ्च beside प्रिय as the other word that travelled in both directions at once.

chapters.title: What You'd Ask For
chapters.label: ch:sa-request-nouns
chapters.canDo: I can name water, milk and food in Sanskrit, say that food is grammatically the eaten thing, and name the three genders every Sanskrit noun carries.

payoff.summary: Say अन्नम्, name the root अद् it shares with खादति's cousin अत्ति, and state the three grammatical genders Sanskrit sorts every noun into, tying the neuter -म् running through the chapter back to the neuter numeral forms of Chapter 6.

chapters.title: The People You'd Introduce
chapters.label: ch:sa-people-nouns
chapters.canDo: I can name a friend, a family, a brother and a sister in Sanskrit, and say which of those words travelled with English and which quietly did not.

payoff.summary: Say भगिनी, name the share-word भग it is built on, name स्वसृ as the real but non-living PIE cousin of English sister, and run the chapter's four people back together with the roads each one travelled.

chapters.title: The Face, Part One
chapters.label: ch:sa-face-nouns-1
chapters.canDo: I can name an eye, an ear and a mouth in Sanskrit, say why eyes take a dual number, and say which of the three words has a settled Western cousin and which do not.

payoff.summary: Say मुखम्, report both scholarly accounts of its origin without choosing between them, and run अक्षि, कर्णः and मुखम् back together against their daughter-language descendants and the neuter gender most of them share.

chapters.title: The Face, Part Two
chapters.label: ch:sa-face-nouns-2
chapters.canDo: I can name a nose and a heart in Sanskrit, say which daughter-language nose-word नासिका is a relative of rather than a parent of, and close the chapter's twelve nouns against the cousin words this book has already shown.

payoff.summary: Say हृदयम्, name the PIE root it shares with heart, cor and kardia, place हृदयम् beside the same root's other independent inheritances, and run all twelve of this tranche's nouns back together by group and by gender.
